title: SQLAlchemy 2.0: mapping, loading strategies and optimistic locking
description: SQLAlchemy 2.0 declarative mapping and SQLModel basics, lazy versus eager loading, N+1 statement counting, the identity map, async pitfalls and version_id_col locking.
source: SQLAlchemy 2.0 documentation (relationship loading techniques, version_id_col, asyncio extension, identity map); SQLModel documentation; FastAPI documentation (handling errors)
seriesDescription: ORM, loading strategies and N+1, transactions, raw SQL, pools and Alembic. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: Complete the SQLAlchemy 2.0 and SQLModel basics.
questions.text: In SQLAlchemy 2.0 a model derives from {1} and declares columns as `id: {2}[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)`. Queries run through `{3}.scalars(select(User))`. A SQLModel class becomes a database table only when it is declared with {4}.
questions.explanation: SQLModel combines Pydantic validation with SQLAlchemy mapping; without table=True a SQLModel class is just a Pydantic schema (useful for request/response models). Session.scalars() returns ORM objects rather than Row tuples.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In SQLAlchemy 2.0 with asyncio, touching an unloaded lazy relationship on an object loaded through AsyncSession raises MissingGreenlet.
questions.reason: SQLAlchemy 2.0 recommends select() with session.scalars() as the primary query style.

whys.a: The recommended query style has nothing to do with why lazy loading fails in async code.
whys.b: Both are true, but R does not explain A: lazy loading fails because it would need implicit blocking I/O inside the event loop.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly says it is false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly says it is false.

questions.explanation: Implicit lazy loading would issue I/O from a plain attribute access, which cannot be awaited. Use selectinload/joinedload up front, await session.refresh(obj, ["rel"]), or AsyncAttrs.awaitable_attrs.

questions.prompt: 12 Book rows belong to 4 distinct Authors. In SQLAlchemy 2.0 with default settings, `books = session.scalars(select(Book)).all()` runs once, then a loop reads the lazy many-to-one `book.author` for all 12 books. How many SELECT statements run in total?
questions.explanation: The Session identity map caches each Author by primary key, so only the first access per distinct author hits the database: 1 + 4 = 5, not 13. (Checked by counting cursor executions on SQLAlchemy.) A one-to-many loop would not have this saving.

questions.prompt: In SQLAlchemy 2.0 with default relationship settings, authors = session.scalars(select(Author).limit(20)).all() runs once, then a loop calls len(a.books) on each of the 20 authors (a lazy one-to-many collection). How many SELECT statements run in total?
questions.explanation: 1 for the authors plus one lazy load per author is 21, the classic N+1. Verified by counting cursor executions. Adding selectinload(Author.books) turns it into 2.

questions.prompt: select(Author).options(selectinload(Author.books)) loads 1,200 authors. selectinload sends its follow-up SELECT ... WHERE author_id IN (...) in chunks of at most 500 parameters. How many SELECT statements run in total, counting the first?
questions.explanation: 1 statement for the authors plus ceil(1200 / 500) = 3 chunked IN queries gives 4. Verified by counting cursor executions on 1,200 authors.

questions.prompt: Models Author and Book exist, with Author.books a one-to-many relationship. Write the SQLAlchemy 2.0 statement `stmt` that selects all authors and loads their books collection with a second SELECT ... WHERE author_id IN (...) rather than a join.
questions.explanation: selectinload suits collections because it avoids the row multiplication of joinedload. joinedload is better for many-to-one. Both avoid the N+1 of the default lazy="select".

questions.prompt: In SQLAlchemy 2.0, `session.scalars(select(Author).options(joinedload(Author.books))).all()` raises InvalidRequestError about a missing unique() call. What is the intended fix?

options.text: Call .unique() on the result, or switch the collection load to selectinload.
options.why: Correct: joined eager loading of a collection repeats the parent in each row, so 2.0 insists on explicit de-duplication.

options.text: Add DISTINCT through session.execute(...).all() because the ORM deduplicates joins implicitly.
options.why: The ORM does not deduplicate here, and plain .all() on the Result is exactly the call that raises the error.

options.text: Set lazy='dynamic' on the relationship so no join is emitted.
options.why: Dynamic loaders are legacy and unsupported with asyncio; they do not fix de-duplication of a joined load.

options.text: Disable the identity map with expire_on_commit=False so rows stay unique.
options.why: expire_on_commit controls attribute expiry after commit and has nothing to do with result de-duplication.

questions.explanation: Because a joined load of a collection returns one row per child, 1.x silently de-duplicated while 2.0 asks you to say so (`.unique()`). For collections prefer selectinload, which avoids the row multiplication.

questions.prompt: Match each SQLAlchemy relationship loading strategy with its behaviour.

right.text: Loads the related rows on first access with a separate SELECT
Runs a second SELECT ... WHERE parent_id IN (...) for all loaded parents
Fetches the related rows in the same statement with a LEFT OUTER JOIN
Raises an error if the relationship is accessed without being loaded
Caches the collection in Redis between requests
Loads related rows in a background thread

questions.explanation: raiseload is a good test-time guard: it turns every accidental lazy load into an exception, which exposes N+1 and async-incompatible lazy access early (verified: it raises InvalidRequestError).

questions.prompt: In a SQLAlchemy 2.0 declarative class Author, write the books relationship (typed with Mapped[list["Book"]]) that is the inverse side of Book.author (back_populates="author") and deletes books removed from the collection or when the author is deleted.
questions.model:
books: Mapped[list["Book"]] = relationship(
    back_populates="author", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
questions.explanation: Verified in a runnable model. The foreign key lives on Book.author_id; the many-to-one side declares back_populates="books" in return. Without delete-orphan, removing a book from the list only clears its foreign key.

questions.prompt: A FastAPI app uses version_id_col for optimistic locking. Register an exception handler on app so that StaleDataError produces HTTP 409 with the JSON body {"error": "conflict"}.
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking detects a conflict; it does not resolve it. The client should reload and re-apply its change. A 412 with an ETag/If-Match flow is an equally valid contract.
questions.starter:
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from sqlalchemy.orm.exc import StaleDataError

questions.prompt: In a SQLAlchemy 2.0 declarative class Product, `version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(default=1)` is already declared. Write the class-level line that tells the ORM to use it for optimistic locking.
questions.explanation: On a stale update the UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? matches 0 rows and the Session raises StaleDataError (checked against SQLAlchemy 2.x). The keyword form __mapper_args__ = dict(version_id_col=version) is equivalent.

questions.prompt: Two users edit the same row. The second save raises StaleDataError from SQLAlchemy. What should a REST API normally do?

options.text: Retry the identical UPDATE in a loop until it succeeds, since the conflict is transient.
options.why: The stale version never matches again, so the loop would never end.

options.text: Return 409 Conflict and let the client reload and re-apply its change.
options.why: Correct: the data changed underneath the client; a person must decide how to merge.

options.text: Return 500 and page the on-call engineer, since it is an unexpected failure.
options.why: It is an expected concurrency outcome and maps to a client-side error.

options.text: Drop version_id_col so later saves silently overwrite the first one.
options.why: That restores the lost-update bug the version column prevents.

questions.explanation: Automatic retry is only safe for server-side read-modify-write that re-reads the row on each attempt.

questions.prompt: Select all valid ways to avoid the N+1 problem when listing authors together with their books in SQLAlchemy 2.0.

options.text: Use selectinload(Author.books) in the query options.
options.why: One extra IN query loads all collections.
It only logs SQL; it does not change the statements.

options.text: Use joinedload(Author.books) and call .unique() on the result.
options.why: One joined statement; unique() removes duplicate parents.
It controls attribute expiry after commit, not how relationships load.

options.text: Select only the columns you need with a join, e.g. select(Author.name, Book.title).join(Author.books).
options.why: Plain rows, no lazy loading, one statement.

questions.explanation: Fix N+1 per use case. Detect it by counting statements in tests or by setting lazy="raise" on relationships.

questions.prompt: True or false: calling session.get(Author, 7) issues no SQL if the Author with primary key 7 is already present in that Session's identity map.

options.why: Correct: Session.get() checks the identity map first and returns the existing object.
Wrong: the identity map caches loaded objects by primary key for the life of the Session, so no SQL is needed.

questions.explanation: Only primary-key lookups use this shortcut; queries with other conditions always go to the database (though they return the existing identity for matching rows).

questions.prompt: True or false: with AsyncSession, reading an unloaded relationship attribute automatically awaits a lazy load and returns the data.

options.why: Wrong: an attribute access cannot be awaited, so the implicit load raises MissingGreenlet.
Correct: use eager loading options up front, await session.refresh(obj, ["rel"]) or AsyncAttrs.awaitable_attrs.

questions.explanation: The same constraint is why many async codebases set lazy="raise" on relationships and expire_on_commit=False on the sessionmaker.
